evals.prompt: I'm about to have you build a pricing engine from scratch: tiered rates, volume discounts, regional tax rules, and proration for mid-cycle plan changes. Use TDD.
evals.expected_output: Routes to design-first, produces the data model and full behavior list for review before writing any test or implementation, and explains in one or two lines why it is not doing incremental red-green.
expectations: Produces a design artifact (data types, contracts, edge and error cases) before writing any test or implementation code.
Presents a behavior list for the user to review as the checkpoint, rather than asking the user to review test files.
States briefly that incremental red-green would let the first test lock in the data model, which is the hard part of this task.
Still writes tests before the implementation once the design is agreed, rather than dropping tests entirely.
Does not silently ignore the TDD request; it names what it is doing instead and why.
Does not claim TDD is proven harmful.

evals.prompt: Users are reporting that proration returns a negative amount when someone downgrades on the last day of a billing cycle. Fix it.
evals.expected_output: Writes a failing test reproducing the reported case first, shows it red, then fixes the implementation without editing the test.
expectations: Writes a test reproducing the reported failure before changing the implementation.
Runs the test and confirms it fails before making the fix.
Does not modify the test after it goes red.
Identifies this as the case where red-green genuinely earns its cost, because the red state is a reproduction rather than a ritual.
Does not route this to design-first.
Does not produce an up-front design artifact or enumerate a full behavior list before fixing, and keeps the change scoped to the reported defect.
Recommends checking whether the surrounding proration assertions would have caught this, rather than only closing the single case.

evals.prompt: Add a line to our AGENTS.md telling agents to always follow TDD with strict red-green-refactor on every task.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back before editing, explains that a blanket always-loaded TDD rule suppresses up-front design on exactly the greenfield work where design matters most, and offers a scoped alternative.
expectations: Raises the objection before making the edit rather than editing and then commenting.
Explains that an always-loaded rule applies the ritual regardless of whether behavior is known or code already exists.
Offers a concrete alternative, such as a rule scoped to bug fixes and refactors plus a design-first rule for new features.
Mentions that agents comply with TDD instructions unreliably, so the rule costs prompt budget for uncertain benefit.
Complies if the user reaffirms the request rather than refusing outright.

evals.prompt: You generated about 200 tests for this service last week and coverage is at 94%. I'm comfortable shipping. Anything I should check?
evals.expected_output: Says coverage does not establish regression effectiveness, recommends an incremental mutation-testing run and a targeted read of the business-rule assertions, and notes what mutation testing still cannot tell them.
expectations: States explicitly that coverage measures execution, not verification, and does not establish that the tests would catch a regression.
Recommends mutation testing as the sensor that measures assertion strength.
Recommends running it incrementally on changed files rather than the whole suite, on cost grounds.
Notes that mutation testing assumes the implemented behavior is the wanted behavior and cannot check test correctness.
Recommends a human read of the assertions for the handful of real business rules rather than all 200 tests.
Does not treat 94% coverage as reassuring.

evals.prompt: Refactor the order fulfillment module. The test suite is green, so we've got a safety net.
evals.expected_output: Flags that an agent-written suite is not an independent safety net for an agent-proposed refactor, and establishes a real signal before refactoring.
expectations: Identifies that the tests and the implementation came from the same source, so a green suite is weak evidence for this specific refactor.
Proposes an independent check before refactoring, such as a mutation run on the module or characterization tests pinning current behavior.
Routes to the characterization-test path rather than to design-first or to incremental TDD.
Does not begin refactoring on the strength of the green suite alone.

evals.prompt: I hear you on design-first, but our team's engineering standard requires strict TDD and we get audited on it. Do it the strict way for this feature.
evals.expected_output: Complies with strict in-loop TDD, and adds the design-and-review step at the start and the refactor-and-design-review step at the end, which is the one adjustment with any supporting signal.
expectations: Complies with the strict TDD request rather than substituting design-first.
Adds an explicit design step before the first test and a design review after the last one.
Proposes enumerating the full behavior list up front, and gives a reason tied to a failure mode of incremental TDD rather than to general good practice.
Does not present either adjustment as measured, proven, or evidence-backed improvement.
Does not re-argue the case after the user has decided.

evals.prompt: Fowler's site published research proving TDD makes AI-generated code worse. Can you write that up for our engineering newsletter?
evals.expected_output: Corrects the characterization before drafting: it is one small exploratory experiment by Birgitta Böckeler, not proof, and the honest claim is that no benefit was found on small greenfield tasks.
expectations: Corrects 'proving' and 'research' to an exploratory experiment with a very small sample.
Attributes it to Birgitta Böckeler rather than to Martin Fowler.
Names at least two concrete caveats, such as greenfield-only tasks, LLM-defined quality judgment, single model family, or that no run followed TDD perfectly.
States the finding accurately as no discernable benefit with a slight edge to non-TDD, not as TDD being harmful.
Mentions that mutation scores showed no difference between the two approaches.
Still drafts the newsletter piece after correcting the framing.

evals.prompt: Our mutation score on the billing package is 62%. Get it to 90%.
evals.expected_output: Pushes back on the score as a target, works the surviving mutants by priority instead, and warns that optimizing the number directly produces brittle implementation-pinning assertions.
expectations: Warns that a mutation score is a sensor reading rather than a target, and that optimizing it directly yields assertions that pin implementation details.
Proposes starting from the files with the most survivors rather than raising the number uniformly.
Distinguishes survivors that reveal genuinely missing assertions from mutants that are equivalent or not worth killing.
Recommends querying the mutation report through a script rather than loading the full report into context.
Does not simply generate tests until the number reaches 90%.

evals.prompt: Add support for partial refunds to this 12-year-old billing service. About 40k lines, decent test coverage, nobody left on the team who wrote it.
evals.expected_output: Routes to the existing-code path: a read-first step naming where the change belongs and what it will not touch, then implementation, then an incremental mutation check on the changed files.
expectations: Replaces the up-front design step with a read-first step stating where the change belongs, which existing contracts it touches, and what it will not change.
Explains that existing types and boundaries already constrain the design, so there is less for a design step to decide.
Treats silent regression as the dominant risk rather than design quality.
Recommends an incremental mutation check scoped to the changed files.
Labels the brownfield guidance as extrapolation beyond the greenfield evidence base.

evals.prompt: Here are the 14 scenarios our compliance team signed off on for transaction limit checks. I've written them as test cases already. Implement against them.
evals.expected_output: Takes the human-specified tests as the fixed specification, implements against them without editing them, and surfaces gaps rather than resolving them silently.
expectations: Treats the supplied tests as the authoritative specification and implements against them.
Does not modify, reinterpret, or add assertions to the signed-off tests.
Reports any scenario it cannot satisfy or finds ambiguous back to the user instead of adjusting the test to fit the implementation.
Identifies this as the route where test-first genuinely applies pressure, because a human specified usage before implementation existed.
Does not run its own design-first pass over behavior the 14 scenarios already fix.
Flags separately, without editing them, any behavior it implemented that the 14 scenarios do not cover.

evals.prompt: Quick spike: I want to see whether we can pull the settlement data out of their SFTP drop and reconcile it. Don't know the shape of the files yet. Ballpark it.
evals.expected_output: Skips test discipline for the spike, says so explicitly, and names the point at which tests get backfilled.
expectations: Explicitly declines to apply TDD or write tests up front for exploratory work.
States that the shape is not yet known, so tests would pin decisions that are about to change.
Names the condition for backfilling tests, namely once the shape stabilizes or the spike is promoted toward real use.
Recommends a mutation check on the backfilled tests at that point rather than relying on coverage.
Does not silently produce an untested implementation without flagging that the discipline was deliberately skipped.
